tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## Objective

Redesign Ocean Above into a **modern, calm, ChatGPT-inspired conversational UI with premium travel-product aesthetics**. The current dark UI reads more like a dense enterprise dashboard (blue-black surfaces, strong dividing lines, rectangular controls, technical details dominating the itinerary). **This is not a border-radius-only task:** improve the visual system, spacing, typography, hierarchy, composition, and interaction quality while preserving all booking requirements.

**Design keywords:** modern minimalism · soft rounded surfaces · restrained neutral palette · subtle depth · generous whitespace · content-first · polished AI-native product.

**Reference / baseline**
- Current app: `frontend/src/app/chat/page.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/shell.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/message-list.tsx`.
- Itinerary components: `frontend/src/components/cards/route-card.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/cards/simple-cards.tsx`.
- Existing tokens/styles: `frontend/src/app/globals.css`, `frontend/src/components/ui/*`.
- Composer / SSE integration: `frontend/src/lib/chat.ts`, `frontend/src/lib/sse.ts`.
- Existing screenshots and visual review: `docs/iterations/04-web/D1/` and `docs/iterations/04-web/F1/`.
- Visual reference: ChatGPT's clean conversation layout and floating composer; Linear-like restraint/typography. **Borrow design principles, not exact branding/assets.**

## Scope / implementation plan

### P1 — Establish a coherent design system
- [ ] Audit existing light and dark colors, radii, borders, shadows, spacing, type scale, and interactive states; define semantic design tokens in the existing Tailwind/CSS architecture.
- [ ] Replace blue-heavy dark surfaces with neutral charcoal/zinc; create an equally polished warm-neutral/light theme. Keep accessible, restrained accent/status colors.
- [ ] Use rounded-xl/2xl/3xl selectively, with low-contrast borders, gentle elevation, and fewer nested panels. Do not apply uniform oversized rounding to everything.
- [ ] Consistent type hierarchy (Geist or Inter if available; avoid heavy caps and excessive bold), readable widths, line-height and whitespace.
- [ ] Preserve visual meaning of status colors (quoted, presented, booked, stale, expired, error) and accessible contrast.

### P1 — Chat-first layout
- [ ] Simplify top navigation and sidebar into quiet, low-contrast surfaces; rounded conversation rows, clear active/hover/focus styles, compact but discoverable tickets/history navigation.
- [ ] Center conversation content with a comfortable max width and generous vertical rhythm. Assistant messages should feel mostly borderless; user bubbles have soft rounded surfaces.
- [ ] Build a floating, rounded chat composer with an integrated send control, good multiline typing, clear busy/disabled/focus states, and safe handling of long messages.
- [ ] On mobile, use a clean collapsible sidebar/drawer; avoid overlays hiding content or composer; handle 360px+ widths and keyboard/safe-area insets.

### P1 — Premium itinerary and booking cards
- [ ] Redesign the quote, confirmation and booked-ticket views with clear **origin → transfers → destination**, a restrained route timeline, readable per-leg distances, total distance, and a prominent total price.
- [ ] Preserve **every leg and transfer city**, full total flight distance and price, and the explicit user confirmation action. Never visually imply a ticket has been booked when it is merely quoted/presented.
- [ ] Keep calculation provenance in a **collapsed-by-default** disclosure (still accessible and readable), rather than showing dense Decimal/source details by default.
- [ ] Improve the visual hierarchy for unserved city suggestions, ambiguous city selection, expired/stale quote, error, empty history/tickets states.
- [ ] Keep status copy/buttons fully driven by server state, including loading, post-booking and reconnect/reload. If an existing assistant-text vs status-card discrepancy is reproduced, document and raise it as a functional bug rather than silently changing domain logic.

### P2 — Interaction polish
- [ ] Subtle hover/focus/transition motion only; honor `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- [ ] Responsive density, 44×44px touch targets where applicable, keyboard navigation and visible focus rings.
- [ ] Ensure streamed messages and cards do not cause major layout jumps or unwanted scroll-to-bottom.
- [ ] Reuse existing components and dependencies; no unnecessary animation/UI framework.

## Non-goals / safety constraints

- **Frontend visual and interaction changes only**. Do not change `locations.db`, routing/pricing, LLM prompts, tool contracts, auth, quote state machine, nonce, API shape, or booking permissions.
- No added payment/real-flight features, no MCP/Phoenix work in this issue.
- Do not introduce fake departures, durations or airport metadata absent from `locations.db`.
- Preserve existing light/dark theme functionality; coordinate with existing theme/hydration issue #37 if it affects the implementation.
- Preserve the take-home's explicit route + distance + price confirmation requirement.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Desktop (1440px), tablet (~768px), and mobile (390px and 360px) screenshots demonstrate a cohesive modern minimalist design in **both light and dark themes**.
2. Quote, confirmation, booking success, no-service, ambiguous-city, stale/expired, tickets and history flows are visually checked; calculations are collapsed initially but remain easy to expand.
3. No horizontal overflow, clipped text, obscured composer or touch targets; keyboard/focus/contrast/reduced-motion checks pass.
4. Existing component tests, front-end build and end-to-end booking/history flows still pass. Re-check SSE streaming, confirmation button, book-once semantics and state on refresh.
5. Update relevant design tokens/components and add before/after screenshots and a short design rationale to the existing `docs/iterations/04-web/` review artifacts (or a new dated subfolder). Include raw coding-agent sessions in `prompt history/` per submission requirements.
6. Review actual browser screenshots, not only static mockups. Use the existing visual audit/critique workflow.

## Suggested scheduling

Treat as a **standalone UI polish iteration after functional/runtime correctness fixes**. Start with design tokens + one representative chat/quote screen, review it in both themes, then apply the system to other pages/cards. Prefer a focused PR that can be reviewed without touching backend business logic.

# DESIGN — ocean-above

Single source of truth for visual and interaction rules. Only the coordinator edits this file; user decisions
are written here with their date.

## 1. Character
A calm, trustworthy airline booking assistant: a chat where the user types what they want, and the app
answers with precise, checkable facts — every leg, transfer city, distance and price laid out as a clear
itinerary card before anything is booked. Booked tickets and past conversations are always one click away.
It refuses: decorative gradients and illustrations, numbers that only appear in free text (prices and
distances always also appear in a structured card), a "book" action that is not an explicit confirmation,
and colour that means two things.

## 2. Colour
Direction: **A "Timetable"** (user decision 2026-11-23): a quote reads like a printed airline timetable entry — the
itinerary block (service line, one row per leg with right-aligned tabular distances, "Transfer at X" rows, double
rule above the totals, price as the largest figure) is the signature. Source and alternatives:
`docs/iterations/04-web/D1/design-proposal.md`.

Strategy: restrained, plus a committed shell. Neutral surfaces with a cool tint, one accent, and status colours
that always come with text or an icon. Contrast ratios below were computed with the WCAG formula.

| Token | Value | Use | Contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#F3F5F7` | page | — |
| `surface` | `#FFFFFF` | cards, composer | — |
| `rail` | `#E9EDF1` | conversation list, skeletons | — |
| `ink` | `#102030` | text, strong rules | 16.5:1 on surface, 15.1:1 on ground |
| `ink-2` | `#4A5866` | secondary text | 7.3:1 on surface, 6.7:1 on ground, 6.2:1 on rail |
| `hairline` | `#CBD3DB` | 1 px dividers (decorative) | 1.5:1 (not used for meaning) |
| `field` | `#8794A1` | input borders | 3.1:1 (non-text ≥ 3:1) |
| placeholder | `#5E6B78` | input placeholder | 5.5:1 |
| `shell` | `#0E2F4A` | header band | white 13.8:1, inactive tab `#B7C9D9` 8.1:1 |
| `accent` | `#0B5D8F` | primary button, focus ring, links, service line, selection | white on accent 7.1:1 |
| `accent-tint` | `#DDE8F2` | user message, text selection | ink on it 13.3:1 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#1A6B34` / `#E6F4EA` | Booked, ticket | 5.8:1 |
| `warn` / `warn-bg` | `#7A4A00` / `#FFF1D6` | needs your attention: awaiting confirmation, no service, similar names, notice | 6.7:1 |
| `danger` / `danger-bg` | `#B42318` / `#FDECEA` | expired, out of date, errors | 5.8:1 (6.6:1 on white) |

Each colour has one meaning:
- amber means "your attention or action is needed";
- green means "booked";
- red means "cannot proceed";
- blue means "act here".

The "Hub" badge is neutral (it used to be green).

### Dark palette
The dark palette is a re-mix, not an inversion. Surfaces are deep navy; the accent is lightened, and text on
accent-coloured buttons turns dark. Ratios below were computed with the WCAG 2.x formula.

| Token | Dark value | Contrast |
|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#0C1721` | — |
| `surface` | `#15232F` | — |
| `rail` | `#101D29` | — |
| `ink` | `#E6EDF3` | 13.5:1 on surface, 15.3:1 on ground |
| `ink-2` | `#A3B3C2` | 7.5:1 on surface, 8.4:1 on ground, 8.0:1 on rail |
| placeholder | `#8A9BAB` | 5.6:1 |
| `hairline` | `#2A3B4A` | decorative |
| `field` | `#5F7486` | 3.3:1 (non-text) |
| `shell` | `#0A2236` | white 16.2:1; inactive tab `#9FB6CA` 7.7:1 |
| `accent` | `#4BA3DB` | 5.8:1 on surface; text on it `#06131D` 6.8:1 |
| `accent-tint` | `#1D3A52` | ink on it 10.0:1 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#6FD08C` / `#12301E` | 7.6:1 |
| `warn` / `warn-bg` | `#F2B84B` / `#3A2A0A` | 7.7:1 |
| `danger` / `danger-bg` | `#FF8A7A` / `#3D1714` | 6.9:1 (7.0:1 on surface) |

On the navy header the focus ring is white in both themes (13.8:1 and 16.2:1).

**How the theme is chosen:**
- With nothing stored, `:root` uses the light tokens, and `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` switches to dark on
  `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`.
- A stored choice sets `<html data-theme>` from an inline `<head>` script before the body is parsed, so there is no
  flash.
- The switch is `components/theme-toggle.tsx`: three `aria-pressed` buttons. It sits in the header on desktop, and
  in the settings menu (gear icon) and on the login page on phones.

## 3. Type, spacing, shape
- **Family:** Public Sans, variable 100–900, loaded with `next/font/google` (self-hosted at build time, `display: swap`, CSS variable `--font-public-sans`). It has `tnum`, which turns on
  tabular figures for every number (`.figures`). The fallback is the system UI stack. One family carries everything.
- **Scale (rem / px, fixed, ratio about 1.2):**

  | Step | px / line height | Use |
  |---|---|---|
  | xs | 12 / 16 | badges, column heads (uppercase, +0.06em), timestamps |
  | sm | 14 / 20 | card body, legs, list rows |
  | 15 | 15 / 24 | chat messages |
  | base | 16 / 24 | inputs (avoids iOS zoom) |
  | lg | 18 / 24 | card titles (`Guangzhou → Lima`) |
  | xl | 22 / 28 | the price |
  | 2xl | 28 / 36 | page titles |

- **Weights:** 400 body, 500 legs and nav, 600 titles and buttons, 700 price and page titles.
- **Spacing:** 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24, plus 32 for page padding on desktop. Card padding is 16 px (20 px from `sm` up).
  The message gap is 20 px.
- **Touch targets:** ≥ 44×44 (`min-h-11 min-w-11` on every button, link and list row).
- **Radii:**
  - 4 px: badges, inline code;
  - 6 px: buttons, inputs, notices;
  - 8 px: cards;
  - 12 px: the user message (4 px at the tail corner).
- **Lines:**
  - 1 px hairline: dividers and card borders;
  - 1 px ink: the column-head rule;
  - 3 px double ink: the rule above the totals;
  - 2 px accent: the border of a card awaiting confirmation;
  - 3 px: the active tab underline.
- **Shadow:** none on cards. Only the mobile drawer has one (`8px 0 24px rgba(16,32,48,.18)`).
- **Layout:**
  - the chat column is at most 768 px, centred, and cards at most 448 px;
  - assistant text has no bubble (it reads as prose) and user text has a tinted bubble;
  - the desktop conversation rail is 288 px and becomes a drawer below 768 px.

## 4. Motion
- **Durations:** 150 ms for hover and colour, 200 ms for card enter (opacity plus 4 px rise) and the drawer slide.
  Easing is `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` (ease-out).
- **Reduced motion:** every duration becomes 0 and no loop runs.
- **Loops:** the only indeterminate indicator is the three-dot "typing" pulse shown while a reply streams (1.2 s);
  the skeleton blocks pulse while loading. Nothing else loops. The countdown changes its text once a second and is
  not animated.

## 5. Components
These are shadcn/ui-style primitives copied into `frontend/src/components/ui/`, with no Radix and no new npm
packages. App components wrap them.

| Layer | Component | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ui | `Button` | variants: default (accent), outline, ghost, link; all ≥ 44 px; focus ring 2 px accent |
| ui | `Card` | flat sheet, 1 px hairline, 8 px radius |
| ui | `Badge` | tones: muted, ok, warn, danger; always text, optional icon |
| ui | `Input` | 44 px, `field` border, accent focus |
| ui | `Skeleton`, `Alert` | tinted strip plus icon; tones warn and danger |
| icons | `icons.tsx` | lucide-react named imports wrapped once (20 px, 1.75 stroke, `aria-hidden`) |
| app | `ThemeToggle` | System / Light / Dark, `aria-pressed`, 44 px |
| app | `ItineraryBlock` (`Route` in `route-card.tsx`) | the signature: service line, leg rows, transfer rows, double rule, totals |
| app | `QuoteCard` / `BookingRequestCard` | status badge plus countdown; accent border while confirmable; Confirm, error, Get a new quote; calculation details (chevron disclosure) |
| app | `TicketCard`, `TicketList` | green "✓ Ticket t_…" badge, booked time in English |
| app | `NoServiceCard` | amber "No service" badge, headline, nearest served cities in the distance column (first in bold) |
| app | `AmbiguousCityCard` | candidates as ruled rows, "Flies to …" |
| app | `UnknownCityCard`, `NoticeCard` | quiet text card; amber notice strip with icon |
| app | `Message` / `MessageList` | user bubble; assistant prose; typing status |
| app | `ConversationList`, drawer | rail on desktop, drawer with close button on phones |
| app | `Shell` | navy band, tabs, sign-out (icon only on phones) |
| app | `LoadingState`, `EmptyState`, `ErrorState` | skeleton cards; teaching empty state; red strip with Retry |

## 6. Screens
### Chat
1. Hierarchy: the newest card, then the assistant text, then the composer.
2. Primary action: **Confirm booking** on a confirmable card. The card gets a 2 px accent border, and the button
   spans the card's full width directly under the price.
3. Empty state:
   - "Where would you like to fly?";
   - one sentence promising that every leg, the distance and the price appear before booking;
   - three example prompts that fill the input (they do not send).
4. Errors:
   - booking errors appear inside the card (red strip with icon), with "Get a new quote" when needed;
   - stream and network errors appear as a red strip with Retry above the composer.

### My tickets
1. Hierarchy: the page title, a one-line explanation, then ticket cards (2 columns from `lg`).
2. Primary action: none. The page is read-only; booking happens in Chat.
3. Empty state: "You have no tickets yet. Book a flight in Chat and it will appear here."
4. Error: a red strip with Retry.

### History
1. Hierarchy: the page title, then conversation rows (title, preview, time).
2. Primary action: open a conversation. The detail view is the read-only chat with no Confirm.
3. Empty state: "No conversations yet."
4. Error: a red strip with Retry. A missing conversation shows "not found" text.

### Login
1. Hierarchy: the product name, one line of purpose, then the form.
2. Primary action: Sign in.
3. Error: inline text under the form.
4. Navy band with the theme switch, then the "Sign in" card.

## 7. Exceptions (dated)
- 2026-11-23: **superseded direction.** The user replaced direction A "Timetable" with issue #39 (ChatGPT-inspired soft
  minimalism: neutral charcoal/zinc dark, warm-neutral light, floating composer, selective rounding, calculation details
  collapsed). Sections 2–6 will be rewritten from the 07-ui proposal once the user confirms it; until then they
  describe the shipped UI. #39 is the source of truth for new UI work.
- 2026-11-23: direction A "Timetable"; Public Sans via `next/font/google`; lucide-react icons (named imports); light + dark
  themes following the system with a System / Light / Dark switch; markdown rendered by our own minimal renderer
  (streamdown removed for bundle size: 353 → 206 KB gzip).
- 2026-11-23: mobile is first-class (≥ 360 px wide, no horizontal scroll); screenshots at desktop + mobile.
- 2026-11-23: numbers are shown rounded (distance 1 decimal km, price to the cent) but always computed and
  stored exact.
- 2026-11-23: UI is reviewed with Impeccable (critique / audit / detect); its findings that conflict with this
  file go to the user as a design-conflicts table.
- <YYYY-MM-DD: decision, why, limits.>

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

<!-- Source of the answers: the coordinator's brief for issue #20 (2026-11-23), plus AGENTS.md, docs/design/design.md
and the take-home brief. No interactive interview took place; nothing below is invented beyond those sources. -->

## Platform

web

## Users
- **Travellers** (primary): ordinary passengers of the airline Ocean Above who want to book a flight by typing what they
  want ("I want to fly from Guangzhou to Lima"), check the route and price, and later look up their tickets. They use
  a desktop browser or, just as often, a phone.
- **Take-home reviewers**: engineers evaluating the demo (`ocean-above.potafree.net`, or `docker compose up` locally).
  They read the design doc, try edge cases (unserved cities, ambiguous names, refusing to confirm) and check that every
  number on screen is right and that nothing is booked without an explicit confirmation.

## Product Purpose
A natural-language flight booking assistant for Ocean Above. Core jobs:
1. Ask for a flight in plain language and get a quote: the cheapest route with every leg, every transfer city, the
   total distance and the price.
2. Check that full route, distance and price, then book by clicking an explicit confirm control.
3. Look up booked tickets (in chat or on My tickets).
4. Re-read any past conversation (History).
Success: the user can verify every fact before paying, and a reviewer finds no number that does not come from the
backend's deterministic computation.

## Positioning
The language model only understands and phrases; routes, distances, prices, nearest served cities and bookings are
computed by deterministic backend code from `locations.db`. Every number shown comes from a tool result, and booking
happens only when the user clicks a one-time confirm card. The interface makes that split visible: facts live in
structured cards, not in chat prose.

## Operating Context
- Chat screen: conversation list (drawer on phones), messages with streamed assistant text, and cards: quote,
  booking request (confirm), ticket, ticket list, no-service (nearest served cities), ambiguous city (candidates with
  distinguishing facts), unknown city, notice.
- My tickets and History (read-only conversations) pages; a simple login (fixed dev account; Google later).
- Quotes expire; a booking can be refused as stale / expired / busy / data unavailable and the UI must say what to do.

## Capabilities and Constraints
- Numbers are shown only from the backend's `*_display` fields; the frontend never formats or recomputes numbers.
- Quote and confirm cards must make the legs, transfer cities, total distance and price prominent (take-home req. 7).
- Unserved city → tell the user and show the nearest served city (req. 8).
- Nothing is booked without the user clicking confirm on that exact quote; the LLM cannot book.
- Mobile is first-class: ≥ 360 px wide, touch targets ≥ 44×44, no horizontal scroll.
- Stack: Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS; shadcn/ui-style components copied into the repo. Minimal dependencies.
- English UI copy.

## Brand Commitments

## Objective

Redesign Ocean Above into a **modern, calm, ChatGPT-inspired conversational UI with premium travel-product aesthetics**. The current dark UI reads more like a dense enterprise dashboard (blue-black surfaces, strong dividing lines, rectangular controls, technical details dominating the itinerary). **This is not a border-radius-only task:** improve the visual system, spacing, typography, hierarchy, composition, and interaction quality while preserving all booking requirements.

**Design keywords:** modern minimalism · soft rounded surfaces · restrained neutral palette · subtle depth · generous whitespace · content-first · polished AI-native product.

**Reference / baseline**
- Current app: `frontend/src/app/chat/page.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/shell.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/message-list.tsx`.
- Itinerary components: `frontend/src/components/cards/route-card.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/cards/simple-cards.tsx`.
- Existing tokens/styles: `frontend/src/app/globals.css`, `frontend/src/components/ui/*`.
- Composer / SSE integration: `frontend/src/lib/chat.ts`, `frontend/src/lib/sse.ts`.
- Existing screenshots and visual review: `docs/iterations/04-web/D1/` and `docs/iterations/04-web/F1/`.
- Visual reference: ChatGPT's clean conversation layout and floating composer; Linear-like restraint/typography. **Borrow design principles, not exact branding/assets.**

## Scope / implementation plan

### P1 — Establish a coherent design system
- [ ] Audit existing light and dark colors, radii, borders, shadows, spacing, type scale, and interactive states; define semantic design tokens in the existing Tailwind/CSS architecture.
- [ ] Replace blue-heavy dark surfaces with neutral charcoal/zinc; create an equally polished warm-neutral/light theme. Keep accessible, restrained accent/status colors.
- [ ] Use rounded-xl/2xl/3xl selectively, with low-contrast borders, gentle elevation, and fewer nested panels. Do not apply uniform oversized rounding to everything.
- [ ] Consistent type hierarchy (Geist or Inter if available; avoid heavy caps and excessive bold), readable widths, line-height and whitespace.
- [ ] Preserve visual meaning of status colors (quoted, presented, booked, stale, expired, error) and accessible contrast.

### P1 — Chat-first layout
- [ ] Simplify top navigation and sidebar into quiet, low-contrast surfaces; rounded conversation rows, clear active/hover/focus styles, compact but discoverable tickets/history navigation.
- [ ] Center conversation content with a comfortable max width and generous vertical rhythm. Assistant messages should feel mostly borderless; user bubbles have soft rounded surfaces.
- [ ] Build a floating, rounded chat composer with an integrated send control, good multiline typing, clear busy/disabled/focus states, and safe handling of long messages.
- [ ] On mobile, use a clean collapsible sidebar/drawer; avoid overlays hiding content or composer; handle 360px+ widths and keyboard/safe-area insets.

### P1 — Premium itinerary and booking cards
- [ ] Redesign the quote, confirmation and booked-ticket views with clear **origin → transfers → destination**, a restrained route timeline, readable per-leg distances, total distance, and a prominent total price.
- [ ] Preserve **every leg and transfer city**, full total flight distance and price, and the explicit user confirmation action. Never visually imply a ticket has been booked when it is merely quoted/presented.
- [ ] Keep calculation provenance in a **collapsed-by-default** disclosure (still accessible and readable), rather than showing dense Decimal/source details by default.
- [ ] Improve the visual hierarchy for unserved city suggestions, ambiguous city selection, expired/stale quote, error, empty history/tickets states.
- [ ] Keep status copy/buttons fully driven by server state, including loading, post-booking and reconnect/reload. If an existing assistant-text vs status-card discrepancy is reproduced, document and raise it as a functional bug rather than silently changing domain logic.

### P2 — Interaction polish
- [ ] Subtle hover/focus/transition motion only; honor `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- [ ] Responsive density, 44×44px touch targets where applicable, keyboard navigation and visible focus rings.
- [ ] Ensure streamed messages and cards do not cause major layout jumps or unwanted scroll-to-bottom.
- [ ] Reuse existing components and dependencies; no unnecessary animation/UI framework.

## Non-goals / safety constraints

- **Frontend visual and interaction changes only**. Do not change `locations.db`, routing/pricing, LLM prompts, tool contracts, auth, quote state machine, nonce, API shape, or booking permissions.
- No added payment/real-flight features, no MCP/Phoenix work in this issue.
- Do not introduce fake departures, durations or airport metadata absent from `locations.db`.
- Preserve existing light/dark theme functionality; coordinate with existing theme/hydration issue #37 if it affects the implementation.
- Preserve the take-home's explicit route + distance + price confirmation requirement.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Desktop (1440px), tablet (~768px), and mobile (390px and 360px) screenshots demonstrate a cohesive modern minimalist design in **both light and dark themes**.
2. Quote, confirmation, booking success, no-service, ambiguous-city, stale/expired, tickets and history flows are visually checked; calculations are collapsed initially but remain easy to expand.
3. No horizontal overflow, clipped text, obscured composer or touch targets; keyboard/focus/contrast/reduced-motion checks pass.
4. Existing component tests, front-end build and end-to-end booking/history flows still pass. Re-check SSE streaming, confirmation button, book-once semantics and state on refresh.
5. Update relevant design tokens/components and add before/after screenshots and a short design rationale to the existing `docs/iterations/04-web/` review artifacts (or a new dated subfolder). Include raw coding-agent sessions in `prompt history/` per submission requirements.
6. Review actual browser screenshots, not only static mockups. Use the existing visual audit/critique workflow.

## Suggested scheduling

Treat as a **standalone UI polish iteration after functional/runtime correctness fixes**. Start with design tokens + one representative chat/quote screen, review it in both themes, then apply the system to other pages/cards. Prefer a focused PR that can be reviewed without touching backend business logic.

# DESIGN — ocean-above

Single source of truth for visual and interaction rules. Only the coordinator edits this file; user decisions
are written here with their date.

## 1. Character
A calm, trustworthy airline booking assistant: a chat where the user types what they want, and the app
answers with precise, checkable facts — every leg, transfer city, distance and price laid out as a clear
itinerary card before anything is booked. Booked tickets and past conversations are always one click away.
It refuses: decorative gradients and illustrations, numbers that only appear in free text (prices and
distances always also appear in a structured card), a "book" action that is not an explicit confirmation,
and colour that means two things.

## 2. Colour
Direction: **A "Timetable"** (user decision 2026-11-23): a quote reads like a printed airline timetable entry — the
itinerary block (service line, one row per leg with right-aligned tabular distances, "Transfer at X" rows, double
rule above the totals, price as the largest figure) is the signature. Source and alternatives:
`docs/iterations/04-web/D1/design-proposal.md`.

Strategy: restrained, plus a committed shell. Neutral surfaces with a cool tint, one accent, and status colours
that always come with text or an icon. Contrast ratios below were computed with the WCAG formula.

| Token | Value | Use | Contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#F3F5F7` | page | — |
| `surface` | `#FFFFFF` | cards, composer | — |
| `rail` | `#E9EDF1` | conversation list, skeletons | — |
| `ink` | `#102030` | text, strong rules | 16.5:1 on surface, 15.1:1 on ground |
| `ink-2` | `#4A5866` | secondary text | 7.3:1 on surface, 6.7:1 on ground, 6.2:1 on rail |
| `hairline` | `#CBD3DB` | 1 px dividers (decorative) | 1.5:1 (not used for meaning) |
| `field` | `#8794A1` | input borders | 3.1:1 (non-text ≥ 3:1) |
| placeholder | `#5E6B78` | input placeholder | 5.5:1 |
| `shell` | `#0E2F4A` | header band | white 13.8:1, inactive tab `#B7C9D9` 8.1:1 |
| `accent` | `#0B5D8F` | primary button, focus ring, links, service line, selection | white on accent 7.1:1 |
| `accent-tint` | `#DDE8F2` | user message, text selection | ink on it 13.3:1 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#1A6B34` / `#E6F4EA` | Booked, ticket | 5.8:1 |
| `warn` / `warn-bg` | `#7A4A00` / `#FFF1D6` | needs your attention: awaiting confirmation, no service, similar names, notice | 6.7:1 |
| `danger` / `danger-bg` | `#B42318` / `#FDECEA` | expired, out of date, errors | 5.8:1 (6.6:1 on white) |

Each colour has one meaning:
- amber means "your attention or action is needed";
- green means "booked";
- red means "cannot proceed";
- blue means "act here".

The "Hub" badge is neutral (it used to be green).

### Dark palette
The dark palette is a re-mix, not an inversion. Surfaces are deep navy; the accent is lightened, and text on
accent-coloured buttons turns dark. Ratios below were computed with the WCAG 2.x formula.

| Token | Dark value | Contrast |
|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#0C1721` | — |
| `surface` | `#15232F` | — |
| `rail` | `#101D29` | — |
| `ink` | `#E6EDF3` | 13.5:1 on surface, 15.3:1 on ground |
| `ink-2` | `#A3B3C2` | 7.5:1 on surface, 8.4:1 on ground, 8.0:1 on rail |
| placeholder | `#8A9BAB` | 5.6:1 |
| `hairline` | `#2A3B4A` | decorative |
| `field` | `#5F7486` | 3.3:1 (non-text) |
| `shell` | `#0A2236` | white 16.2:1; inactive tab `#9FB6CA` 7.7:1 |
| `accent` | `#4BA3DB` | 5.8:1 on surface; text on it `#06131D` 6.8:1 |
| `accent-tint` | `#1D3A52` | ink on it 10.0:1 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#6FD08C` / `#12301E` | 7.6:1 |
| `warn` / `warn-bg` | `#F2B84B` / `#3A2A0A` | 7.7:1 |
| `danger` / `danger-bg` | `#FF8A7A` / `#3D1714` | 6.9:1 (7.0:1 on surface) |

On the navy header the focus ring is white in both themes (13.8:1 and 16.2:1).

**How the theme is chosen:**
- With nothing stored, `:root` uses the light tokens, and `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` switches to dark on
  `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`.
- A stored choice sets `<html data-theme>` from an inline `<head>` script before the body is parsed, so there is no
  flash.
- The switch is `components/theme-toggle.tsx`: three `aria-pressed` buttons. It sits in the header on desktop, and
  in the settings menu (gear icon) and on the login page on phones.

## 3. Type, spacing, shape
- **Family:** Public Sans, variable 100–900, loaded with `next/font/google` (self-hosted at build time, `display: swap`, CSS variable `--font-public-sans`). It has `tnum`, which turns on
  tabular figures for every number (`.figures`). The fallback is the system UI stack. One family carries everything.
- **Scale (rem / px, fixed, ratio about 1.2):**

  | Step | px / line height | Use |
  |---|---|---|
  | xs | 12 / 16 | badges, column heads (uppercase, +0.06em), timestamps |
  | sm | 14 / 20 | card body, legs, list rows |
  | 15 | 15 / 24 | chat messages |
  | base | 16 / 24 | inputs (avoids iOS zoom) |
  | lg | 18 / 24 | card titles (`Guangzhou → Lima`) |
  | xl | 22 / 28 | the price |
  | 2xl | 28 / 36 | page titles |

- **Weights:** 400 body, 500 legs and nav, 600 titles and buttons, 700 price and page titles.
- **Spacing:** 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24, plus 32 for page padding on desktop. Card padding is 16 px (20 px from `sm` up).
  The message gap is 20 px.
- **Touch targets:** ≥ 44×44 (`min-h-11 min-w-11` on every button, link and list row).
- **Radii:**
  - 4 px: badges, inline code;
  - 6 px: buttons, inputs, notices;
  - 8 px: cards;
  - 12 px: the user message (4 px at the tail corner).
- **Lines:**
  - 1 px hairline: dividers and card borders;
  - 1 px ink: the column-head rule;
  - 3 px double ink: the rule above the totals;
  - 2 px accent: the border of a card awaiting confirmation;
  - 3 px: the active tab underline.
- **Shadow:** none on cards. Only the mobile drawer has one (`8px 0 24px rgba(16,32,48,.18)`).
- **Layout:**
  - the chat column is at most 768 px, centred, and cards at most 448 px;
  - assistant text has no bubble (it reads as prose) and user text has a tinted bubble;
  - the desktop conversation rail is 288 px and becomes a drawer below 768 px.

## 4. Motion
- **Durations:** 150 ms for hover and colour, 200 ms for card enter (opacity plus 4 px rise) and the drawer slide.
  Easing is `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` (ease-out).
- **Reduced motion:** every duration becomes 0 and no loop runs.
- **Loops:** the only indeterminate indicator is the three-dot "typing" pulse shown while a reply streams (1.2 s);
  the skeleton blocks pulse while loading. Nothing else loops. The countdown changes its text once a second and is
  not animated.

## 5. Components
These are shadcn/ui-style primitives copied into `frontend/src/components/ui/`, with no Radix and no new npm
packages. App components wrap them.

| Layer | Component | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ui | `Button` | variants: default (accent), outline, ghost, link; all ≥ 44 px; focus ring 2 px accent |
| ui | `Card` | flat sheet, 1 px hairline, 8 px radius |
| ui | `Badge` | tones: muted, ok, warn, danger; always text, optional icon |
| ui | `Input` | 44 px, `field` border, accent focus |
| ui | `Skeleton`, `Alert` | tinted strip plus icon; tones warn and danger |
| icons | `icons.tsx` | lucide-react named imports wrapped once (20 px, 1.75 stroke, `aria-hidden`) |
| app | `ThemeToggle` | System / Light / Dark, `aria-pressed`, 44 px |
| app | `ItineraryBlock` (`Route` in `route-card.tsx`) | the signature: service line, leg rows, transfer rows, double rule, totals |
| app | `QuoteCard` / `BookingRequestCard` | status badge plus countdown; accent border while confirmable; Confirm, error, Get a new quote; calculation details (chevron disclosure) |
| app | `TicketCard`, `TicketList` | green "✓ Ticket t_…" badge, booked time in English |
| app | `NoServiceCard` | amber "No service" badge, headline, nearest served cities in the distance column (first in bold) |
| app | `AmbiguousCityCard` | candidates as ruled rows, "Flies to …" |
| app | `UnknownCityCard`, `NoticeCard` | quiet text card; amber notice strip with icon |
| app | `Message` / `MessageList` | user bubble; assistant prose; typing status |
| app | `ConversationList`, drawer | rail on desktop, drawer with close button on phones |
| app | `Shell` | navy band, tabs, sign-out (icon only on phones) |
| app | `LoadingState`, `EmptyState`, `ErrorState` | skeleton cards; teaching empty state; red strip with Retry |

## 6. Screens
### Chat
1. Hierarchy: the newest card, then the assistant text, then the composer.
2. Primary action: **Confirm booking** on a confirmable card. The card gets a 2 px accent border, and the button
   spans the card's full width directly under the price.
3. Empty state:
   - "Where would you like to fly?";
   - one sentence promising that every leg, the distance and the price appear before booking;
   - three example prompts that fill the input (they do not send).
4. Errors:
   - booking errors appear inside the card (red strip with icon), with "Get a new quote" when needed;
   - stream and network errors appear as a red strip with Retry above the composer.

### My tickets
1. Hierarchy: the page title, a one-line explanation, then ticket cards (2 columns from `lg`).
2. Primary action: none. The page is read-only; booking happens in Chat.
3. Empty state: "You have no tickets yet. Book a flight in Chat and it will appear here."
4. Error: a red strip with Retry.

### History
1. Hierarchy: the page title, then conversation rows (title, preview, time).
2. Primary action: open a conversation. The detail view is the read-only chat with no Confirm.
3. Empty state: "No conversations yet."
4. Error: a red strip with Retry. A missing conversation shows "not found" text.

### Login
1. Hierarchy: the product name, one line of purpose, then the form.
2. Primary action: Sign in.
3. Error: inline text under the form.
4. Navy band with the theme switch, then the "Sign in" card.

## 7. Exceptions (dated)
- 2026-11-23: **superseded direction.** The user replaced direction A "Timetable" with issue #39 (ChatGPT-inspired soft
  minimalism: neutral charcoal/zinc dark, warm-neutral light, floating composer, selective rounding, calculation details
  collapsed). Sections 2–6 will be rewritten from the 07-ui proposal once the user confirms it; until then they
  describe the shipped UI. #39 is the source of truth for new UI work.
- 2026-11-23: direction A "Timetable"; Public Sans via `next/font/google`; lucide-react icons (named imports); light + dark
  themes following the system with a System / Light / Dark switch; markdown rendered by our own minimal renderer
  (streamdown removed for bundle size: 353 → 206 KB gzip).
- 2026-11-23: mobile is first-class (≥ 360 px wide, no horizontal scroll); screenshots at desktop + mobile.
- 2026-11-23: numbers are shown rounded (distance 1 decimal km, price to the cent) but always computed and
  stored exact.
- 2026-11-23: UI is reviewed with Impeccable (critique / audit / detect); its findings that conflict with this
  file go to the user as a design-conflicts table.
- <YYYY-MM-DD: decision, why, limits.>

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

<!-- Source of the answers: the coordinator's brief for issue #20 (2026-11-23), plus AGENTS.md, docs/design/design.md
and the take-home brief. No interactive interview took place; nothing below is invented beyond those sources. -->

## Platform

web

## Users
- **Travellers** (primary): ordinary passengers of the airline Ocean Above who want to book a flight by typing what they
  want ("I want to fly from Guangzhou to Lima"), check the route and price, and later look up their tickets. They use
  a desktop browser or, just as often, a phone.
- **Take-home reviewers**: engineers evaluating the demo (`ocean-above.potafree.net`, or `docker compose up` locally).
  They read the design doc, try edge cases (unserved cities, ambiguous names, refusing to confirm) and check that every
  number on screen is right and that nothing is booked without an explicit confirmation.

## Product Purpose
A natural-language flight booking assistant for Ocean Above. Core jobs:
1. Ask for a flight in plain language and get a quote: the cheapest route with every leg, every transfer city, the
   total distance and the price.
2. Check that full route, distance and price, then book by clicking an explicit confirm control.
3. Look up booked tickets (in chat or on My tickets).
4. Re-read any past conversation (History).
Success: the user can verify every fact before paying, and a reviewer finds no number that does not come from the
backend's deterministic computation.

## Positioning
The language model only understands and phrases; routes, distances, prices, nearest served cities and bookings are
computed by deterministic backend code from `locations.db`. Every number shown comes from a tool result, and booking
happens only when the user clicks a one-time confirm card. The interface makes that split visible: facts live in
structured cards, not in chat prose.

## Operating Context
- Chat screen: conversation list (drawer on phones), messages with streamed assistant text, and cards: quote,
  booking request (confirm), ticket, ticket list, no-service (nearest served cities), ambiguous city (candidates with
  distinguishing facts), unknown city, notice.
- My tickets and History (read-only conversations) pages; a simple login (fixed dev account; Google later).
- Quotes expire; a booking can be refused as stale / expired / busy / data unavailable and the UI must say what to do.

## Capabilities and Constraints
- Numbers are shown only from the backend's `*_display` fields; the frontend never formats or recomputes numbers.
- Quote and confirm cards must make the legs, transfer cities, total distance and price prominent (take-home req. 7).
- Unserved city → tell the user and show the nearest served city (req. 8).
- Nothing is booked without the user clicking confirm on that exact quote; the LLM cannot book.
- Mobile is first-class: ≥ 360 px wide, touch targets ≥ 44×44, no horizontal scroll.
- Stack: Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS; shadcn/ui-style components copied into the repo. Minimal dependencies.
- English UI copy.

## Brand Commitments
- Name: **Ocean Above** (fictional airline from the take-home). No logo or brand assets exist.
- Character (DESIGN.md §1): calm, trustworthy, precise; no decorative gradients or illustrations; prices and distances
  always also appear in a structured card; colour never means two things.

## Evidence on Hand
- `locations.db` (cities, hubs, links) and the contract fixtures in `contract/fixtures/` (realistic quotes, tickets,
  conversations). No testimonials, customers or marketing claims exist and none may be invented.

## Product Principles
1. Facts before prose: anything the user must verify is in a structured card.
2. Confirmation is explicit and unmistakable; its state (awaiting, booked, expired, out of date) is always legible.
3. Every failure says what happened and what to do next.
4. Phone and desktop are equals.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

alone; reduced motion respected.

import sys
def L(h):
    h=h.lstrip('#'); c=[int(h[i:i+2],16)/255 for i in (0,2,4)]
    c=[x/12.92 if x<=0.03928 else ((x+0.055)/1.055)**2.4 for x in c]
    return 0.2126*c[0]+0.7152*c[1]+0.0722*c[2]
def cr(a,b):
    x,y=sorted([L(a),L(b)],reverse=True); return (x+0.05)/(y+0.05)
for line in sys.stdin:
    line=line.strip()
    if not line: continue
    name,fg,*bgs=line.split()
    print(f"{name:28s} {fg} " + "  ".join(f"{bg}:{cr(fg,bg):.2f}" for bg in bgs))

`ego-browser skill > "$env:TEMP\ego-browser-skill.md"` in PowerShell.

## References

content.content:
1	[ego-browser:skill] ego-browser usage guide v2.2.1 (macos)
2	
3	# ego-browser
4	
5	Call `help()` or `help("page.click")` to print signatures and uncommon options of APIs named below; it prints by itself, so do not wrap it in `console.log`. For installation or connection problems, read `references/install.md` in the ego-browser Skill directory and follow its link for your operating system.
6	
7	## Run browser scripts
8	
9	Pass the script to `ego-browser nodejs`.
10	
11	```bash
12	ego-browser nodejs <<'EOF'
13	const task = await taskSpace("inspect example page");
14	const page = task.page("p1");
15	await page.goto("https://example.com");
16	
17	console.log({ taskSpaceId: task.spaceId, page: page.label });
18	console.log(await page.snapshot());
19	EOF
20	```
21	
22	When a sandbox blocks heredoc input, use `ego-browser nodejs -e '<code>'` instead. Use single quotes around the code and double quotes for JavaScript strings; single quotes within the code require shell quoting.
23	
24	The script always runs in Node.js, not in the web Page. Browser helpers and Node.js APIs belong in the script; Page globals such as `window`, `document`, `location`, and DOM APIs do not. Put browser-side JavaScript inside `page.evaluate()`. Do not import Playwright or launch another browser.
25	
26	The Node.js runtime uses ESM. When a script needs local files, load built-ins with dynamic imports such as `await import("node:fs/promises")`. The script does not run in your shell's working directory, so use absolute paths for every file it reads or writes. It also does not inherit your shell's environment variables: `process.env` will not contain values you set before running `ego-browser`, so write every input directly into the script.
27	
28	Ego-browser exposes a small custom API. It is not Playwright, even where names and options look similar. Use only the TaskSpace, Page, FileChooser, mouse, and keyboard APIs listed in this Skill. Do not infer methods such as `locator()`, `getByRole()`, `context()`, `expect()`, or `route()`. When the listed API does not cover an operation, use `page.evaluate()` or `page.cdp()` instead of guessing another method.
29	
30	Only these pointer actions accept an optional `label` option: `click()`, `dblclick()`, `hover()`, `dragAndDrop()`, `mouse.click()`, `mouse.move()`, and `mouse.wheel()`. Pass a concise 3-6 word description to keep the action text next to the visible agent cursor in sync with the action. Other methods, such as `fill()`, `press()`, `focus()`, `selectOption()`, `waitForSelector()`, `keyboard.*()`, `mouse.down()`, and `mouse.up()`, reject a `label` option. The `label` in `selectOption(selector, { label })` is different: it selects the option whose visible text matches.
31	
32	When the user explicitly asks for ego-browser, start with a real browser command and diagnose the CLI or installation only if it fails.
33	
34	## Spaces, rounds, and pages
35	
36	- One user goal keeps one TaskSpace across your replies while that space exists. Use multiple spaces only when the user explicitly requests them.
37	- Start and end each reply's browser work as described in "Starting and ending a reply" below. Task space names are unique; prefer the numeric id once you have it.
38	- Never use a new TaskSpace to recover from a stuck, blocked, timed-out, or unexpected Page. Recover within the existing space; if it cannot continue, stop and ask the user.
39	- Every invocation starts a new Node.js process. Task spaces, tabs, and Page labels persist; JavaScript variables do not.
40	- A new task space starts with Page `p1`; navigate it instead of opening another Page.
41	- Reuse a Page with `goto()` instead of opening a new Page for every URL.
42	- All time values are milliseconds.
43	
44	Do not inspect or select profiles unless the user explicitly requests a particular Ego Lite profile. A `profileId` applies only when creating a space; use `help("profiles")` for the exact workflow.
45	
46	Supported TaskSpace API:
47	
48	- State: `spaceId`, `name`, `ownership`, `page(label)`, `userPage()`
49	- Pages: `await task.pages()`, `await task.tabs()`, `newPage()`, `adopt(page, { as? })`, `release(label)`
50	- Control: `waitForControl(options)`, `handOff()`, `finish({ keep })`
51	- Advanced: `cdp(method, params, options)`
52	
53	Pages receive permanent labels such as `p1`, `p2`, and `p3`. Prefer these labels to custom `{ as }` values. Reuse or close Pages as the task proceeds; the runtime reports the configured Page budget when it is reached.
54	
55	`task.page(label)` only refers to a Page that already exists; it never creates one, and its handle is always truthy, so `task.page("p2") || await task.newPage()` and `if (!page)` do not detect a missing label. Use labels printed by earlier output or by `await task.pages()`. When multiple Pages must stay open, call `await task.newPage()` for another blank Page and navigate it with `goto()`.
56	
57	`await task.pages()` returns managed Pages. `await task.tabs()` returns every tab in the space as `{ label?, page, targetId, title, url, active, openedBy }`. A tab without a label is unmanaged; adopt it before operating:
58	
59	```js
60	const active = (await task.tabs()).find((item) => item.active);
61	if (active && !active.label) {
62	  const page = await task.adopt(active.page);
63	  console.log({ page: page.label, url: await page.url() });
64	}
65	```
66	
67	`release(label)` returns an unknown-origin Page to the user without closing its tab. Close Agent-created Pages with `page.close()`. Treat `openedBy: "unknown"` as user-owned when deciding whether a Page may be closed.
68	
69	## Page operations
70	
71	Page API:
72	
73	- State and observation: `label`, `spaceId`, `openedBy`, `targetId`, `url()`, `title()`, `info()`, `snapshot()`, `screenshot()`
74	- Navigation and waits: `goto()`, `reload()`, `waitForURL()`, `waitForEvent()`, `waitForSelector()`, `waitForLoadState()`, `waitForFunction()`, `waitForTimeout()`
75	- Elements: `click()`, `dblclick()`, `hover()`, `dragAndDrop()`, `fill()`, `selectOption()`, `focus()`, `press()`, `setInputFiles()`, `waitForFileChooser()`, `close()`
76	- Dialogs: `acceptDialog(promptText?)`, `dismissDialog()`
77	- Pointer: `mouse.click()`, `move()`, `down()`, `up()`, `wheel()`
78	- Keyboard: `keyboard.down()`, `up()`, `press()`, `type()`, `insertText()`, `paste()`
79	- Page code and protocols: `evaluate(fnOrString, argument)`, `fetch(url, options)`, `cdp(method, params, options)`, `events()`
80	
81	`page.evaluate()` callbacks run only inside the Page; they cannot read variables or Node.js modules from the surrounding script. Define browser-side helpers inside the callback or pass one JSON-serializable value as its second argument.
82	
83	`goto()` and `reload()` stop a navigation that has not committed by their timeout, so the Page stays usable on its previous document; retry with a longer timeout. Any other call on a Page whose navigation is pending (after a link click, for example) waits one bounded period, then fails with `EGO_PAGE_UNRESPONSIVE` and stops that navigation; the error says which document the Page shows now and how to load the pending one. `evaluate()` reports the same outcome as `EGO_PAGE_EVALUATION_TIMED_OUT` with `stopped` set.
84	
85	Work efficiently:
86	
87	- Each time you observe, collect only the cheapest page state sufficient to choose the next action. Use a snapshot for semantic or locator ground truth and a screenshot for visual confirmation; do not request both by default.
88	- If an action does not produce the expected result, inspect the current page before deciding whether to retry. Do not blindly repeat it or immediately fall back to coordinates or raw CDP.
89	- Once the page clearly shows the requested result, stop; do not confirm the same result through multiple surfaces.
90	
91	### Semantic pages: snapshot and selectors
92	
93	Prefer snapshots and semantic selectors for ordinary DOM pages. Use screenshots and coordinates only when useful DOM semantics are unavailable.
94	
95	Before choosing an unfamiliar target, take a snapshot. When the current state is sufficient to plan several actions on the same Page, complete them in one script invocation, then observe the result once. Observe between actions only when an intermediate result changes what should happen next. Keep the action sequence, the wait for its final expected state, and the next snapshot in the same script invocation. Print the snapshot last so the next round can act on it directly. The final snapshot is the next round's starting view of the changed page; without it, that round usually has to spend a separate browser call observing before it can choose the next target, which wastes compute.
96	
97	Wait for the expected result: use `waitForURL()` for navigation, `waitForSelector()` for element state, or `waitForFunction()` for application state. Avoid fixed delays when an observable condition exists. Actions stop waiting for a missing target once the page is idle, so `waitForSelector()` first when an element is expected later. A snapshot captures the current moment; it does not wait for the page to become stable. `page.snapshot()` captures the current viewport. For content outside it, use `page.snapshot({ scope: "full_page" })`. When the document scrolls past the viewport, the snapshot ends with a `[more content below the viewport: ...]` line: nodes are omitted, not absent. If the expected result may land below the fold, scroll or use `full_page` before concluding it did not appear.
98	
99	The default viewport snapshot includes visible iframe content returned by the browser. To focus on a frame's subtree, reuse the ref printed on its `iframe` line:
100	
101	```js
102	console.log(await page.snapshot({ scope: "subtree", root: "@12" }));
103	```
104	
105	Use the refs returned by the subtree for actions inside the iframe. A subtree snapshot does not scope later locator actions; they still prefer actionable matches in the top document before searching frames.
106	
107	`waitForLoadState()` defaults to `load`. `waitForFunction()` takes Playwright's args (`undefined` before options if no arg) but returns `true`, not the predicate's value:
108	
109	```js
110	await page.waitForFunction(() => window.ready, undefined, { timeout: 5000 });
111	```
112	
113	```js
114	// Next round: act using the previous output, verify, then prepare the next round.
115	const page = task.page("p1");
116	await page.fill("@21", "user@example.com");
117	await page.click("loc=role:button[name='Sign in']");
118	await page.waitForSelector("loc=css:#account-home", { state: "visible" });
119	console.log(await page.snapshot());
120	```
121	
122	Element actions accept:
123	
124	- snapshot refs such as `@21` or `ref=21`
125	- `text=...` for page content
126	- `loc=css:`, `loc=role:`, and `loc=href:` locators
127	- `xpath=...`
128	- raw CSS selectors
129	
130	Selector actions require exactly one match. Unquoted text normalizes whitespace, ignores case, and matches a substring; quoted text such as `text="Save changes"` is exact and case-sensitive.
131	
132	A small Playwright-compatible selector subset is also accepted: `css=...`, terminal `:has-text("...")` and `:text-is("...")`, `>> nth=N` after a CSS, text, or href selector (`N` is `-1` or non-negative), plus `loc=role:...[name*="..."]` for accessible-name substrings. Other Playwright selector syntax is not supported.
133	
134	When a selector identifies a wrapper, `focus()` and `press()` may use its interactive ancestor or unique editable descendant; `fill()` and `setInputFiles()` only continue to a unique compatible control.
135	
136	`click()`, `fill()`, `hover()`, and `dragAndDrop()` automatically bring their target into view with browser wheel input, falling back to a programmatic scroll when the wheel does not move the target. Do not pre-scroll solely to make a DOM target actionable.
137	
138	Snapshot node names are accessibility roles. Use a ref now or `loc=...` to find the element again. After the page changes, take a new snapshot. When a useful node has no ref, construct a selector from its role, text, or surrounding context. CSS searches nested open shadow roots. Actions use an actionable match in the top document first, then search frames when the top document has none. Multiple actionable matches in the selected document or frame are ambiguous.
139	
140	Select options by value, visible label, or zero-based index. A string matches either value or label; pass an array for a multiple select:
141	
142	```js
143	await page.selectOption("select[name=month]", { label: "October" });
144	```
145	
146	Pass `null` or `[]` to clear the current selection.
147	
148	### Visual pages: screenshot, mouse, and keyboard
149	
150	Use a screenshot with mouse and keyboard operations for canvas, rich-text, spreadsheets, maps, and other interfaces that lack useful DOM semantics:
151	
152	```js
153	const path = await page.screenshot({ path: "/absolute/path/before.png" });
154	await page.mouse.click(420, 260, { label: "open spreadsheet cell" });
155	await page.mouse.wheel(0, 600, { label: "scroll project board" });
156	await page.keyboard.paste("hello\tworld");
157	console.log({ screenshot: path });
158	```
159	
160	`path` must be absolute; relative paths are rejected. Omit `path` to write into the system temporary directory and use the returned file path.
161	
162	Inspect the screenshot with an image-viewing tool. Coordinates use CSS pixels; keyboard names and `+`-separated chords follow Playwright syntax. Use `ControlOrMeta` for portable shortcuts and verify the resulting page state. `mouse.wheel()` performs a short wheel-input motion at the current mouse position and resolves when that motion completes. In each script invocation, move or click over the intended scrollable area before using it.
163	
164	On macOS and Windows, `keyboard.paste()` sends the native paste shortcut and then restores the user's clipboard. Pass `{ text, html }` when a rich editor needs structured clipboard content; `text` is the plain-text fallback. On other platforms, use `keyboard.insertText()` for plain text.
165	
166	For rich-text editors and editable grids, validate a small edit before repeating it at scale. Canvas-backed editors may not expose visible content through DOM text or selectors; verify those results with a screenshot or an application-specific visible state.
167	
168	`page.screenshot()` can sometimes fail after about 15s with `EGO_PAGE_UNRESPONSIVE` on `Page.captureScreenshot`, even if `page.evaluate()` still works. Retry at most once. For a canvas, read its pixels through `page.evaluate()` with `canvas.toDataURL("image/png")` (tainted canvases throw; WebGL may read blank).
169	
170	### Page JavaScript and CDP
171	
172	Use `page.evaluate()` for bulk extraction or complex in-page work. It returns a JSON-serializable value:
173	
174	```js
175	const rows = await page.evaluate(
176	  ({ selector, limit }) =>
177	    [...document.querySelectorAll(selector)].slice(0, limit).map((node) => ({
178	      text: node.textContent?.trim(),
179	      href: node.querySelector("a")?.href,
180	    })),
181	  { selector: "article", limit: 20 },
182	);
183	```
184	
185	`page.evaluate()` has no timeout option. Keep long work in bounded calls; on a safety timeout, use `executionStopped` and `mayHaveLateEffects` to decide whether an unsafe follow-up requires reloading or closing the Page first.
186	
187	Use documented Page methods first. If a wrapper is missing or does not work reliably on the current page, use `page.cdp()` as a lower-level path for diagnosis or control. It accepts Page, Runtime, DOM, Network, Input, and similar commands; use `task.cdp()` for Target and Browser commands. Both reject a misplaced `sessionId` in params. Raw CDP invalidates refs. Do not persist `page.targetId` across rounds.
188	
189	## Action receipts, popups, and dialogs
190	
191	When an action is expected to open a new Page, start the wait before the action:
192	
193	```js
194	const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent("popup");
195	await page.click('a[target="_blank"]');
196	const popupPage = await popupPromise;
197	await popupPage.waitForLoadState();
198	```
199	
200	High-level actions also report immediately observed popups in `receipt.popups` as `{ label, targetId }`. Resolve the Page with `task.page(receipt.popups[0].label)` and continue there; wait for its URL when the destination matters.
201	
202	Page sessions hide page console messages from CDP so sites cannot detect the automation. To read `Runtime.consoleAPICalled` while debugging, first call `await page.cdp("egoAutomated.disable")`, then `page.cdp("Runtime.enable")`. Sites can detect CDP again while it is off.
203	
204	A synchronous JavaScript dialog may appear as `receipt.dialog` or in `page.info()`. Handle it before continuing:
205	
206	```js
207	await page.acceptDialog("prompt response");
208	// Or: await page.dismissDialog();
209	```
210	
211	A receipt describes only the dispatched action and immediate popup or dialog observations; it does not verify the resulting application state.
212	
213	## Files and requests
214	
215	Set an existing file input with absolute paths:
216	
217	```js
218	await page.setInputFiles("input[type=file]", ["/absolute/path/report.pdf"]);
219	```
220	
221	If a click creates the file input, start waiting before the click:
222	
223	```js
224	const chooserPromise = page.waitForFileChooser({ timeout: 10_000 });
225	await page.click("button.upload");
226	const chooser = await chooserPromise;
227	const result = await chooser.setFiles("/absolute/path/report.pdf");
228	```
229	
230	An upload-triggered JavaScript dialog may be returned as `result.dialog`; when present, handle it with the dialog methods above.
231	
232	For a browser download, arm the event before the triggering action and save the returned artifact to an absolute path in the same script:
233	
234	```js
235	const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent("download", { timeout: 30_000 });
236	await page.click("button.download");
237	const download = await downloadPromise;
238	console.log({
239	  url: download.url(),
240	  suggestedFilename: download.suggestedFilename(),
241	});
242	await download.saveAs("/absolute/path/report.pdf");
243	```
244	
245	`download.saveAs()` waits for completion and creates missing parent directories. `download.path()` returns the round-local temporary file; `failure()`, `cancel()`, and `delete()` manage its lifecycle. Temporary download files are removed when the SDK round is disposed, so call `saveAs()` before the script ends. Do not set a download directory with raw CDP; the download wait manages the browser's single shared download setting.
246	
247	`page.fetch()` runs `window.fetch()` in the Page: relative URLs, cookies, and service workers use that Page, and browser CORS still applies. It returns `{ ok, status, statusText, url, headers, body }`:
248	
249	```js
250	const response = await page.fetch("/api/items", {
251	  method: "POST",
252	  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
253	  body: JSON.stringify({ limit: 20 }),
254	  timeout: 10_000,
255	});
256	```
257	
258	Save binary responses without converting them to text:
259	
260	```js
261	await page.fetch("/image.png", { saveAs: "/absolute/path/image.png" });
262	```
263	
264	Use standard Node.js `fetch()` for background requests that do not need Page browser semantics.
265	
266	## Starting and ending a reply
267	
268	Begin the first script of each reply by choosing the space. A new goal gets a new space. A user message that continues an earlier goal, such as a further question, a correction, or a request to continue, continues in that goal's space if it still exists, whatever state your last reply left it in:
269	
270	```js
271	const SPACE_ID = 7; // printed by your last reply about this goal; null for a new goal
272	const entry =
273	  SPACE_ID === null
274	    ? undefined
275	    : (await listTaskSpaces()).find((s) => s.id === SPACE_ID);
276	const task = !entry
277	  ? await taskSpace("descriptive goal name") // new goal, or the earlier space was closed
278	  : entry.ownership === "user"
279	    ? await claimTaskSpace(SPACE_ID) // you finished it with kept Pages
280	    : entry.ownership === "agentDelegatedToUser"
281	      ? await takeOverTaskSpace(SPACE_ID) // control is with the user
282	      : await taskSpace(SPACE_ID); // still in your control
283	// After a claim, no tab has a label yet: adopt the tab you kept.
284	const page =
285	  (await task.pages())[0] ?? (await task.adopt((await task.tabs())[0].page));
286	console.log({
287	  taskSpaceId: task.spaceId,
288	  page: page.label,
289	  tabs: await task.tabs(),
290	});
291	```
292	
293	`finish()` ends all Page labels, kept Pages included. Until you claim a space you finished with kept Pages, neither `taskSpace()` nor `takeOverTaskSpace()` can resume it. After the claim, adopt each tab you kept and use the label `adopt()` returns.
294	
295	End each reply's browser work with one `finish()` in a separate last script, run after earlier output has shown that the request is done, and wait for it before you report. A space finished too early must not take more work in this reply:
296	
297	```js
298	const task = await taskSpace(7); // the taskSpaceId printed earlier in this reply
299	// Default: close the space, including tabs you kept in an earlier reply.
300	await task.finish({ keep: [] });
301	
302	// Exception, instead of the default: keep only the result Page for the user.
303	await task.finish({ keep: ["p2"] });
304	```
305	
306	Keeping Pages is a rare exception: retain only necessary Pages when the user explicitly asks, or when the result must remain in the browser for the user to view or continue working with. Pages merely visited, search results, and intermediate steps do not need to remain open.
307	
308	After `finish()`, do not operate any Page in the same script.
309	
310	## User control
311	
312	Stop when the user takes control or the space is inactive or unassigned. Do not retry or route around the stop. Permission prompts, device choosers, and other browser-owned prompts require the user to handle them.
313	
314	When the user must act in the browser (login without credentials the user gave, CAPTCHA or human verification, 2FA, or other manual step), call `await task.handOff()`, end the round, and explain what they should do. Do not guess credentials or work around it silently. After the user confirms, resume the same space:
315	
316	```js
317	const task = await takeOverTaskSpace(7);
318	const userPage = task.userPage();
319	```
320	
321	Adopt `userPage` if it is unmanaged. Use `waitForControl()` only when the current script must wait in place.
322	
323	Claim any other user-owned or inactive space only when the user explicitly asks; the space you finished for the current goal is claimed as in "Starting and ending a reply".
324	
325	User-created and unknown-origin tabs are protected; if any remain, `keep: []` does not close the whole space, and the script output says so. Tabs you kept in an earlier reply stay yours after a claim and do not block closing. The blank tab that `page.close()` leaves when it closes the last Page is SDK-owned and never blocks closing. Do not close unwanted Pages one by one at completion; list the Pages to keep instead. Do not call `finish()` when the task stops for user control or an error.
326	
327	If the final output contains `[ego-browser:notice]`, finish the current browser task, tell the user an Ego Lite update is available, and run `ego-browser upgrade` only with their approval. Run `ego-browser skill` again after the upgrade.
328	
329	## Clearing cookies, cache, and storage
330	
331	Before clearing any cookie, cache, or storage, read `references/clearing-state.md` in the ego-browser Skill directory. Some clears reach the whole browser profile.
332	
333	[ego-browser:skill] end of guide v2.2.1
